newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: World solar conference kicks off in Zimbabwe.
newsitem.headline: World solar conference kicks off in Zimbabwe.

text.p: Delegates from more than 100 nations begin a two-day conference in Zimbabwe on Monday to champion the use and development of solar and other renewable sources of energy.

Joint conference organisers Zimbabwe and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) say 5,000 delegates, including 22 heads of state and governments, will attend the historic meeting at which about 300 projects will be presented.

The projects, including the desalination of water from the Red Sea for drinking water in Jordan and several plans to provide African villages with solar-powered cookers, are part of a 1996-2005 World Solar Programme prepared by UNESCO.

The Harare conference is also set to discuss possible private industry and donor support for these and other projects, although its organisers say the emphasis will remain that of mobilising global political backing for the greater use of solar, wind and other renewable sources of energy.

UNESCO Director-General Federico Mayor and host Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe say these sources are generally cheaper, environmentally-friendly and easily accessible if mass produced, and the quick solution for 2.4 billion people currently living without electricity worldwide.

"All the technologies that we can develop and transfer, or all the funding that we can provide, indeed all our efforts to promote the development and use of solar energy will bear few tangible results without the necessary political will," Mugabe said at the weekend.
"The need for a strong political will to underscore our commitment to the development of solar energy has long been recognised," he said of the Monday summit called up to drum up such support.

According to the United Nations, about 18 percent of the globe's primary energy currently comes from renewable sources, but UNESCO says greater use could push this figure to between 25 and 35 percent by the year 2050.

UNESCO's Mayor says the adoption of the solar programme would also boost social and economic development, help cut pollution from fossil fuels, avoid the potential dangers of nuclear power plants and reduce the threat of desertification caused by the stripping of Third World forests for firewood.

He proposed on Saturday the formation of an executive council to supervise the World Solar Programme, warning that the continued exclusion of millions of people from modern life could breed extremism and promote instability.
The secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity, Salim Ahmed Salim, told reporters the solar programme would be seriously pursued on the continent.
"I know that it is difficult to have all the people in Africa use solar energy now but I definitely feel that in the long run this will be achievable," he said.
The September 16-17 World Solar Summit is running concurrently with a solar technology exhibition.
